name: Jaw advancement for sleep apnea (MAD devices)
lead: A mandibular advancement device (MAD), also called a mandibular advancement splint, sleep apnea mouth guard or oral appliance, is a mouthpiece worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward. It is prescribed to treat snoring and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a condition in which the airway repeatedly collapses during sleep.[1][2] Its link to looks is indirect: by keeping the airway open overnight it aims at quieter, more continuous sleep, and sleep quality is something appearance communities tie to skin, puffiness and energy for training.

The forward jaw position the device uses is also a topic in looksmaxxing because jaw projection and airway space are discussed together. Small or recessed lower jaws are listed among the craniofacial risk factors for OSA, and jaw advancement surgery (maxillomandibular advancement) both widens the airway and changes the facial profile, with studies of patient satisfaction after the operation.[18][19] The device itself holds the jaw forward only while it is worn, and no published trial has tested it as an appearance treatment.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine recommend oral appliances for primary snoring and for people with OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP or prefer another therapy.[1] Randomized trials have compared MADs with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), and cephalometric follow-up studies describe small changes to tooth position and bite after years of wear.[3][4][8][16]

angle.goal: Sleep quality, airway and jaw posture

angle.text: The device is a medical treatment for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea rather than a facial-aesthetics tool; its benefit is airway patency during sleep. People in appearance communities interested in jaw position and airway see it as one route to better sleep, and as the non-surgical counterpart to jaw-advancement surgery.

paras: Mandibular advancement devices are two-piece or single-piece splints that fit over the upper and lower teeth. Wikipedia describes the mandibular advancement splint as a custom-made prescription mouthpiece worn during sleep, used for obstructive sleep apnea, snoring and some temporomandibular disorders.[1] Many devices are adjustable, allowing the clinician to advance the lower jaw in steps; one randomized trial compared different protrusion positions at a constant vertical dimension.[6] Another study used sleep endoscopy with a simulated bite to predict outcomes.[7]

Obstructive sleep apnea is the most common sleep-related breathing disorder, with repeated partial or full collapse of the airway during sleep.[18] Reference sources list obesity as the main risk factor but note that 20 to 25 percent of patients are not overweight, and that a small lower jaw can displace the tongue backward and narrow the airway.[18]

Wikipedia explains that moving the lower jaw forward tightens soft tissue and muscles of the upper airway, which helps prevent collapse during sleep and reduces the vibration that causes snoring.[1] The effect lasts only while the device is worn.

Craniofacial structure matters to who has apnea. Wikipedia's OSA article lists mandibular hypoplasia (a small lower jaw) and a narrow upper jaw as risk factors, which is the reason jaw position features in discussions of the airway.[18]

A randomized crossover trial compared one month each of CPAP and MAD therapy on cardiovascular and other health outcomes in OSA.[3] Another crossover trial compared 8 weeks of each treatment in 59 patients after polysomnographic titration.[4] A systematic review and meta-analysis compared the effects of CPAP and MADs.[8]

Wikipedia summarizes that devices work better for mild to moderate OSA than severe OSA, that CPAP is generally more efficacious at reducing apneas, that patients often find devices easier to use, that a meta-analysis of 51 randomized trials found oral devices lowered blood pressure in OSA about as well as CPAP, and that a 2024 meta-analysis found about a 66 percent reduction in the apnea-hypopnea index in severe OSA.[1] A review in the European Respiratory Journal discusses MAD therapy as a non-CPAP option.[5] A study of 630 patients examined tolerability and predictors of treatment success.[10]

sections.h: Effects on teeth, bite and facial structure
paras: Long-term wear can move teeth. Wikipedia reports that long-term use has been associated with permanent changes in how the teeth meet and that the devices needed about 0.8 repairs or relines per year.[1] A single-group Japanese study followed 15 adults with mild to moderate OSA for about 4 years and 4 months using cephalograms and dental casts: overjet and overbite each fell by about 1 mm, the upper incisors tipped backward and the lower incisors forward, the mandibular plane angle increased (consistent with a slight clockwise rotation of the lower jaw) and lower anterior face height increased slightly, while SNA, SNB and ANB angles did not change significantly. The authors cautioned that the sample was small and that larger controlled studies are needed.[16]

This is relevant to facial appearance because the device moves the jaw only during sleep; the measured changes concern tooth position and vertical bite relationships, and no study has reported the device improving jaw projection or facial attractiveness.[16]

Wikipedia lists dry mouth, tooth pain, dental discomfort and jaw pain as common issues; many users stop because of discomfort, poor results or a switch to CPAP, and concerns about the effect on teeth are among the factors that reduce adherence.[1] Long-term use was not linked to temporomandibular disorders in the source Wikipedia cites.[1]

Cheaper devices are widely sold without a prescription. Wikipedia says they are unproven and that some sleep specialists consider them potentially dangerous; a 2008 study it cites found that a thermoplastic over-the-counter device could not be recommended as a therapeutic option.[1] Customised devices from a dentist generally cost more, with an out-of-pocket figure of around $1,900 in the United States and insurance often covering the device for CPAP-intolerant patients or moderate OSA.[1]

Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) moves both upper and lower jaws forward permanently. Wikipedia describes it as one of the most effective surgical treatments for sleep apnea and says it was first used to correct facial skeletal deformities and malocclusion before being applied to OSA; it is usually considered after other treatments have failed.[17]

A 2023 meta-analysis in Cureus of 46 papers and 1,268 patient records reported that 85.6 percent of patients were satisfied with their facial appearance after MMA, 8.6 percent indifferent and 5.8 percent not satisfied; physicians rated 94.2 percent of cases as satisfactory and laypeople 73.2 percent, with the sample predominantly male.[19] The authors defined satisfaction as either an increase in fondness for appearance or indifference to the change.[19] This literature concerns the surgery, not the splint.

Randomized trials and meta-analyses have compared MADs with CPAP in obstructive sleep apnea[3][4][8], and a crossover trial compared two types of oral appliance.[11] An early study examined a Herbst-type mandibular advancement device for sleep apnea.[12] A four-year cephalometric follow-up in 15 patients described small tooth and facial-height changes.[16] Registered trials are examining MADs in heart failure, reflux and treatment-response predictors.[13][14][15] These studies concern sleep apnea outcomes and dental changes. No studies found on MADs for facial appearance.

Community discussion specific to sleep-apnea devices is limited. A looksmax.org poster reported a month of progress photos using an oral appliance alongside tongue-posture training, saying a retruded mandible is fixable, and replies questioned whether the photos showed improvement.[20] Another thread asks for alternatives to a custom infra-oral appliance used in facepulling discussions, where a reply says the method needs an external puller worn many hours a day or maxillofacial surgery.[21] Jaw advancement as a goal is more often discussed through orthodontic functional appliances and orthognathic surgery. Wikipedia notes that cheaper non-prescription devices are unproven and that some specialists consider them potentially dangerous.[1]

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing discussion of sleep-apnea MADs is limited; threads on oral appliances mostly concern orthodontic-style appliances, tongue posture and facepulling for a recessed lower jaw.[20][21]

claims.claim: A night-time jaw-forward device improves airway and sleep, and so looks
claims.believers: Users interested in airway and jaw posture describe jaw-forward appliances as part of improving airway and profile.[20]
claims.experts: Guidelines support oral appliances for snoring and CPAP-intolerant OSA, and trials show they reduce apnea events, with CPAP generally more efficacious.[1][3][8]

claims.claim: Wearing a MAD reshapes the jaw
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster reported a month of oral-appliance progress photos and said a retruded mandible is fixable, though other users disputed the visible change.[20]
claims.experts: A four-year follow-up in 15 patients found small tooth and vertical changes, with SNA, SNB and ANB unchanged; no trial has tested the device for facial appearance.[16]

claims.claim: Cheap boil-and-bite devices work as well as custom ones
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster asks for a cheaper alternative to a custom infra-oral appliance.[21]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that a 2008 study found a thermoplastic over-the-counter device could not be recommended and that some specialists consider such devices potentially dangerous.[1]

claims.claim: Jaw advancement surgery gives both airway and a better profile
claims.believers: Community discussion of jaw advancement often couples airway gains with a stronger jawline.[17]
claims.experts: A 2023 meta-analysis found most patients and physicians rated facial appearance as satisfactory after MMA, with laypeople less often so, and the literature is mostly male patients.[19]

card.summary: A sleep-apnea mouthpiece that pushes the lower jaw forward; well studied for breathing, with no evidence it changes your face.
card.aka: MAD, mandibular advancement splint, oral appliance, sleep apnea mouth guard
card.price: About $1,900 out of pocket (US) for custom devices
card.note: Medical device for sleep apnea; long-term use is associated with changes in how the teeth meet.

quick.overview:
Mandibular advancement devices are mouthpieces worn at night that hold the lower jaw forward to keep the airway open. They are prescribed for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea, often when CPAP is not tolerated.

They are connected to looksmaxxing mainly through interest in jaw position and airway; no study has tested them for changing facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: Holding the jaw forward tightens upper-airway tissues and reduces collapse and vibration during sleep. The effect lasts only while the device is worn.
quick.risks: Reported effects include dry mouth, tooth and jaw pain, and long-term changes in how the teeth meet. Many users stop because of discomfort. Cheap non-prescription versions are unproven, and some specialists consider them potentially dangerous.
